Look for deadlines
Message content and attachments should go after about 30 days unless something like an appeal needs them. "Until the bot is removed" is the longest Stoat allows for other data.
Check whether the code is public
Open-source bots can be checked line by line. For closed-source bots you're relying on what the developer tells you.

02 / Why we look at other bots

On 5 September 2026, Stoat Trust & Safety gave Stoatmod 30 days to remove or redesign the parts that collected or kept data without consent, and we did. The notice quoted Stoat's published Community Guidelines:

If every bot must meet these requirements independently, every bot developer needs to be able to read them. More than two months later they still aren't published, so other developers can't know them and users can't check whether the bots in their servers follow them. bronx, for instance, still keeps per-person message counts with no expiry and ranks people on leaderboards any member can see, which is the kind of “user-level records” Stoat told us aren't allowed.
AutoMod's own website says its developer has been on the Stoat team since 2023, and its support server has Stoat's verified badge. It reads members' messages in every server it's in. Yet as of
its website still has no privacy policy, no terms and no privacy notice telling users what it collects, how long it keeps it, or how to say no or ask for deletion.

All-in-one bot · has a privacy policy · code not public

Kuma describes itself as “Stoat's most advanced all-in-one community and security bot”. To be fair to Kuma, it publishes a detailed privacy policy, lets members view, export and delete their data, says it doesn't keep copies of messages, and deletes some records automatically. Its code isn't public, so everything below comes from Kuma's own website, privacy policy and commands page. We first read them on 6 October 2026 and again on
, when its privacy policy said it was last updated in November 2026.

On Stoat, Kuma's verification now uses its own puzzle, a drawn picture, a rules quiz or a probation period for newcomers, with no Cloudflare captcha and nothing about your connection. Image scanning, which sends images to Google's Vision API, is only available on Discord and Fluxer. Account linking with !link is opt-in.
14 October 2026: Kuma rebuilt its verification on Stoat

Kuma said the changes bring its verification in line with Stoat's guidelines: no IP, VPN or connection checks, hashed IP addresses from earlier verifications deleted, its own browser check in place of the Cloudflare captcha, and no use of other servers' reports on Stoat. Its November privacy policy still says all of this. We welcome it, and we see Kuma dropping Cloudflare Turnstile as a step in the right direction.

Kuma has removed cross-server flagging and IP checks on Stoat, just as we did. Its bridging still sends members' messages to other platforms on an admin's decision alone. If the same standard applies to every bot, Stoat should say so publicly. If it doesn't, it should explain what makes the cases different.

Bridge bot · open source · has a privacy policy

bolt links channels on Stoat with channels on other platforms so the same conversation appears in both. It still supports Stoat and was last updated on 18 November 2026. To be fair to bolt, it publishes a privacy policy with a contact for data requests and its code is open source. When we read its code in October, its database stored message IDs rather than message content. Its legal page, which shows no date, lists the data it may collect more broadly: message content and metadata, user information, user activity and IP addresses, stored on hardware in the United States with encrypted backups on Microsoft OneDrive. The main problem is consent.

Stoat required us to get each person's consent before their content was sent to an outside service, and told us that neither a server owner's choice nor a privacy policy counts as consent. A bridge sends members' messages to other platforms on the strength of an admin's choice and a privacy policy alone. If the rule we were held to applies to every bot, bridged channels need a way for each member to agree before their messages are sent off Stoat. Stoat has told another developer it's still deciding its policy on bridge bots.
Logging bot · code not public

log_it's privacy page, last edited on 15 September 2024, says it collects server and channel IDs and all event activity across every server it's in, records each server it joins in its support server, and sends error data to Sentry. Its transparency page says it stores deleted and edited messages with their content, and that most events end up in a local

file that is backed up frequently. The privacy page says everything is deleted when the bot is removed, but not the log file, and gives no retention period for it. Its developers publish the website's code but not the bot's, so we can't check what it actually does. Nothing had changed when we checked on

These three bots were created by the same developer on the same day, 15 June 2023, and all point to one support server, Bot Central. We looked for public information about them on 2 October 2026 and found almost none. There's still no website, policy or code to re-check.

Public docs don't tell us exactly how a bot works today, what it really keeps, what consent it gets or whether Stoat has looked at it. Similar features don't mean identical processing either. What the examples do show is why everyone needs a clear rule that applies to similar behaviour. If you run one of these bots and something here is out of date,
tell us
and we'll correct it.
04 / What Stoat has said
Opt-in, 30 days for content, and privacy policies on the way.
As of

, Stoat hasn't published developer guidelines for bots. Its legal page lists only its general terms, privacy policy and community guidelines, and the last policy update on its updates page was on 30 June 2026. So the most detailed answers are still the ones below, which bronx's developer got from Stoat Trust & Safety and shared with us on 10 October 2026. We've summarised each question and quoted Stoat's answer.
Stoat's answers to bot developers

Stoat is asking every bot to use opt-in for data tied to a person, including per-person stats and rankings. Message content and attachments should be kept for 30 days unless there's a specific reason, such as a case under appeal. Other operational data can be kept while it's needed, at most until the bot is removed. Privacy policies will become a requirement, with a migration period once the guidelines are published. Stoat hasn't decided on bridge bots yet.
